note: Best available answers for four gaps in src/data/gaps.ts. The central kerb-concentration estimate is handled by the modelling team and is not duplicated here. Every number below is either quoted from a source I opened (verified true) or derived by arithmetic shown in the 'arithmetic' fields from such numbers. Nothing is invented.

answers.question: How much does a Taiwanese scooter emit per minute at idle?
answers.bestAnswer: A warm scooter idling at a red light gives off about 1 gram of carbon monoxide and about 0.17 gram of unburnt fuel vapour (hydrocarbons) every minute (60.9 and 10.3 g/h), as measured on common 4-stroke scooters in Hanoi; Taiwan's legal idle limit for scooters built from 2017 allows up to about the same CO.
answers.bestAnswerZh: 一輛已經暖車的機車在紅燈前怠速，每分鐘大約排出 1 公克一氧化碳和約 0.17 公克未燃燒的油氣（碳氫化合物）（每小時 60.9 與 10.3 公克）；這是在河內量到的常見四行程機車數字，而台灣 2017 年後出廠機車的法定怠速上限，允許的一氧化碳也差不多是這個量。

range.co_g_per_h: about 14 (well-tuned catalyst scooter at 0.5% CO) to about 120 (old scooter at the 4.5% legal limit); central 61 (Hanoi mean)
range.hc_g_per_h: about 2 (190 ppm) to about 75 (9000 ppm legal limit for pre-2004 builds); central 10 (Hanoi mean)
range.nox_g_per_h: about 1.8 (Hanoi mean); not scaled for Taiwan

arithmetic: Central: Hanoi mean idle rates 60.9 g/h CO, 10.3 g/h HC, 1.8 g/h NOx, 534.3 g/h CO2, fuel 180 g/h (Nguyen et al. 2021, 5 common models). Per 90 s: 60.9 x 90/3600 = 1.52 g CO; 10.3 x 90/3600 = 0.26 g HC.

Cross-check against Taiwan's own legal idle test (gazette): idle fuel 180 g/h x (1 + 14.7 air/fuel) = 2.83 kg/h exhaust = about 97 mol/h = about 36 L/min at standard conditions (the Italian PEMS paper reports an idle exhaust flow of about 30 L/min for its motorcycles, same order). CO at 2.0% (limit for builds from 2017) = 97 x 0.02 x 28 g/mol = 55 g/h; at 3.5% = 96 g/h; at 4.5% = 123 g/h; at 0.5% = 14 g/h. HC at 1000 ppm (as hexane) = 97 x 0.001 x 86 = 8.4 g/h; at 1600 ppm = 13.4 g/h; at 9000 ppm = 76 g/h.

Back-calculation: the Hanoi mean 60.9 g/h CO corresponds to about 2.2% CO and 10.3 g/h HC to about 1200 ppm, i.e. right at Taiwan's 2017-and-later limits (2.0% / 1000 ppm). So the Hanoi mean is a plausible central value for a Taiwanese scooter that is at or just under the limit, and a conservative (high) value for a new catalyst scooter.

Real Taiwanese idle readings exist: a New Taipei analysis of about 1.13 million inspection records (late 2016) was reported by a search summary to show 4-stroke scooters about 5 years old averaging about 0.9% CO and about 190 ppm HC and the oldest averaging about 3.1% CO. I could NOT open that PDF (server returned 400), so these are listed as unverified in needsManualFetch. If confirmed, 0.9% CO is about 25 g/h and 190 ppm is about 1.6 g/h, which would make 61 g/h CO a high-side central value for newer scooters.
answers.basis: Preference 2 (a measurement elsewhere that transfers). It transfers because the Hanoi test used five of the commonest 4-stroke motorcycle models of the same engine class (about 100-125 cc, fuel about 180 g/h) as Taiwan's scooter fleet, and because converting Taiwan's legal idle limits to g/h with the same fuel flow lands on the same figure. It does not transfer exactly: Hanoi tests were laboratory, models and ages differ, and Taiwan's newer scooters have catalysts and fuel injection. Taiwan's government emission inventory (TEDS 12) publishes no idle factor at all; the Institute of Transportation's 2025 intersection study used the 5 km/h factor as a stand-in for red-light idling, which is stated in the report.
sources: Nguyen Y-L T, Le A-T, Nguyen Duc K, Nguyen Duy V, Nguyen C D (2021) A study on emission and fuel consumption of motorcycles in idle mode and the impacts on air quality in Hanoi, Vietnam. Int. J. Urban Sciences 25(4):522-541. doi:10.1080/12265934.2020.1871059 ; abstract opened at https://ideas.repec.org/a/taf/rjusxx/v25y2021i4p522-541.html (figures found: yes)

Ministry of Environment (Taiwan), Standards for Air Pollutant Emissions from Mobile Sources, Executive Yuan Gazette vol. 29 no. 121 (30 June 2023), Art. 6 table, https://gazette.nat.gov.tw/EG_FileManager/eguploadpub/eg029121/ch07/type1/gov60/num36/Eg.pdf (opened by earlier verifier: yes; limits found)

Hung P-Y et al. (2025) 路口交通環境特性對空氣品質影響及改善指引之研訂(2/2), MOTC Institute of Transportation IOT-113-TB006, https://www.iot.gov.tw/uploads/column_entry_file/file/697879c4085777f955e15ddf/%E8%B7%AF%E5%8F%A3%E4%BA%A4%E9%80%9A%E7%92%B0%E5%A2%83%E7%89%B9%E6%80%A7%E5%B0%8D%E7%A9%BA%E6%B0%A3%E5%93%81%E8%B3%AA%E5%BD%B1%E9%9F%BF%E5%8F%8A%E6%94%B9%E5%96%84%E6%8C%87%E5%BC%95%E4%B9%8B%E7%A0%94%E8%A8%82_2.2_.pdf (opened: yes; Ch.4 section 4.2.2 and appendix 2 reply to reviewers: TEDS 12.0 has no idle factor, 5 km/h factor used)
Vojtisek-Lom M et al. (2020) Atmos. Meas. Tech. 13:5827-5843, https://doi.org/10.5194/amt-13-5827-2020 (opened: yes; idle exhaust flow about 30 L/min)
answers.caveat: The 61 g/h is a Hanoi laboratory average for ordinary scooters, not a Taiwanese test; a new catalyst scooter probably emits several times less CO, a worn or badly tuned one up to about twice as much.

answers.question: How much more is emitted when the pack pulls away on green?
answers.bestAnswer: Nobody has put a number on a scooter pack's pull-away, but the evidence agrees it is a short, sharp burst of seconds: engines pour out far more carbon monoxide and fuel vapour for a moment when the throttle opens, while an idling scooter already emits about as much per hour as one cruising at 30 km/h (about 60 versus about 70 grams of CO an hour), so the red light itself is not a quiet moment.
answers.bestAnswerZh: 還沒有人量過機車車陣起步的確切倍數，但證據一致顯示：起步是只有幾秒鐘的猛烈一陣，油門一開，一氧化碳和油氣會瞬間大增；而怠速的機車每小時排出的一氧化碳（約 60 公克）已經接近時速 30 公里行駛時的量（約 70 公克），所以等紅燈本身並不是「安靜」的時刻。

range.multiplier: none defensible: no scooter modal (idle vs acceleration) rate was obtainable from an open source
range.bounds_from_arithmetic: idle about 61 g/h CO (Hanoi) vs cycle-average cruising at 30 km/h about 73 g/h CO (Taiwan, Tsai 2018); so the extra comes only from the seconds of hard acceleration, not from cruising

arithmetic: Moving CO (Taiwanese in-use Phase V 4-stroke scooters, cycle average): 84.3 g CO per litre of fuel / 34.7 km per litre = 2.43 g/km; at 30 km/h = 73 g/h. HC: 29.4 / 34.7 = 0.85 g/km = 25 g/h at 30 km/h versus 10.3 g/h at idle. These cycle averages already include acceleration, so they are the average of cruising and accelerating, not the acceleration rate itself.
Per litre of fuel, idling is richer: 60.9 g CO per 180 g fuel (about 0.24 L) = about 250 g CO per litre, versus 84 g/L cycle average; idling is not the cleanest state.

One Taiwanese measurement of particles: one 4-stroke motorcycle gave 2.07e4 particles/cm3 at idle, 2.35e4 at 15 km/h and 2.60e4 at 30 km/h (Chien and Huang 2010), so idle was about 80% of the 30 km/h level, not a small fraction.

International junction peaks (cars/diesel, not scooters): ultrafine particle number up to 29x free-flow in a diesel test car at pull-away (Goel and Kumar 2015) but PM2.5 mass only about 16% higher (Kumar and Goel 2016) - already in research/redlight/intersection-peaks.json.
answers.basis: No Taiwanese or other scooter study gives idle vs acceleration emission rates in an open source I could read: the Italian PEMS paper confirms qualitatively that 'sharp accelerations after a stop are clearly visible in terms of HC and CO emissions' but gives no rates; Taiwanese chassis-dynamometer theses (NCKU, ECE cycle by mode) probably contain per-mode numbers but the thesis server returned 503. Inventing a multiplier from engine physics would need unsourced engine assumptions, so none is given. What the site can say honestly is the direction (spike real, brief) and the bounded comparison (idle about equals cruising per hour). A modelling team wanting a scenario could treat pull-away as an uncertainty band rather than a number, and only after the NCKU theses are read.
sources: Vojtisek-Lom M, Zardini A A, Pechout M, et al. (2020) A miniature PEMS for real-driving monitoring of motorcycles. Atmos. Meas. Tech. 13:5827-5843, https://doi.org/10.5194/amt-13-5827-2020 (opened: yes; qualitative statement found, no rates)

Tsai J-H, Yao Y-C, Huang P-H, Chiang H-L (2018) Aerosol Air Qual. Res. 18(12):3056-3067, https://doi.org/10.4209/aaqr.2018.07.0264 (abstract-level figures from research/redlight/idle-emissions.json, verified by earlier verifier; I did not reopen)
Nguyen Y-L T et al. (2021) doi:10.1080/12265934.2020.1871059 (opened abstract: yes)
Chien S-M, Huang Y-J (2010) J. Environ. Sci. Health A, https://doi.org/10.1080/10934529.2010.513289 (from earlier verifier; not reopened)
Goel A, Kumar P (2015); Kumar P, Goel A (2016) (from research/redlight/intersection-peaks.json; not reopened)
answers.caveat: This is an honest 'direction and bounds' answer, not a multiplier: the size of the spike for a scooter pack is still unmeasured, and the site should not print any 'x times' figure.

answers.question: How many scooters wait at one red light?
answers.bestAnswer: At a busy Taiwanese junction about 20 to 40 scooters stop on each road during one 90-second red light, and about 5 on a quiet road; pedestrians wait roughly 85 to 115 seconds because the whole signal cycle is 120 to 180 seconds.
answers.bestAnswerZh: 在台灣繁忙的路口，一個 90 秒的紅燈期間，每一條路上大約有 20 到 40 輛機車停下來等，冷清的路口大約 5 輛；整個號誌週期是 120 到 180 秒，行人大約要等 85 到 115 秒。

range.busy_junction_per_road_per_90s_red: about 30 to 37 (measured mean counts at the two busiest Kaohsiung sites, 4,811 and 5,974 scooters/h)
range.pedestrian_wait: cycle 120 s with 34 s pedestrian green and cycle 150 s with 38 s pedestrian green at exclusive-phase sites: red about 86 to 112 s; cycles at other studied junctions 150 to 200 s

arithmetic: Counts: 12-hour mean scooter counts from camera surveys at six Kaohsiung and New Taipei junctions, July 2024: Mingcheng 1st Rd/Minzu 1st Rd 5,974.2 scooters (62% of traffic); Bo'ai 2nd Rd/Mingcheng 2nd Rd 4,810.7 (59.3%); HSR Rd/Chongxin Rd 818.7 (42.1%); the other three between. Unit check: the report gives 6,784 PCU/h for the busiest site and 1,596 PCU/h for the quietest; solving with the same counts gives scooter weights of about 0.43-0.48 PCU, so the counts are per hour (I read the report's '輛次' as vehicles per hour on this basis; the report does not state the unit on the pages I read).

Split over the four approaches equally: 5,974 / 4 = 1,494 per approach per hour. Arrivals during a 90 s red = 1,494 x 90 / 3600 = 37; for the 4,811 site: 30; for the 819 site: 5.1. For a 60 s red: 25, 20, 3.4.

Red length: Kaohsiung Qixian 1st Rd/Minzu 2nd Rd has a 180 s cycle with 90 s green + 4 s yellow + 3 s all-red for the main road, so the other road is stopped about 83-90 s; report shows 120, 150, 180 and 200 s cycles elsewhere.
Pedestrian wait: exclusive pedestrian phase sites: cycle 150 s with 38 s pedestrian green (150-38 = 112 s) and cycle 120 s with 34 s pedestrian green (120-34 = 86 s).
answers.basis: Preference 3 (transparent estimate from measured quantities). The only measured inputs are the Institute of Transportation's own camera counts and signal timings (opened and read). The even split over four approaches understates a main road and overstates a side road; scooters that arrive during the green or that stop in a two-stage turn box are not separated; counts are 12-hour means (peak is higher). No Taiwanese study reporting queue size per cycle was found in open sources: the NYCU/NCTU theses on motorcycle waiting zones (10 junctions in Taipei and Hsinchu, 2,984 video samples) and the Tainan queue-formation study exist but could not be opened.
sources: Hung P-Y, Chen K-N, Su C-T, et al. (2025) 路口交通環境特性對空氣品質影響及改善指引之研訂(2/2), MOTC Institute of Transportation IOT-113-TB006, https://www.iot.gov.tw/uploads/column_entry_file/file/697879c4085777f955e15ddf/%E8%B7%AF%E5%8F%A3%E4%BA%A4%E9%80%9A%E7%92%B0%E5%A2%83%E7%89%B9%E6%80%A7%E5%B0%8D%E7%A9%BA%E6%B0%A3%E5%93%81%E8%B3%AA%E5%BD%B1%E9%9F%BF%E5%8F%8A%E6%94%B9%E5%96%84%E6%8C%87%E5%BC%95%E4%B9%8B%E7%A0%94%E8%A8%82_2.2_.pdf (opened: yes; Ch.3.1.1, 3.1.3, 3.4, 2.2.4 timing tables, 4.3 phase descriptions)

Lan C-L, Chang G-L (2015) A traffic signal optimization model for intersections experiencing heavy scooter-vehicle mixed traffic flows. IEEE Trans. ITS, doi:10.1109/TITS.2014.2376292 (opened: yes; confirms scooters form short, wide queues near the stop line and use waiting areas; no per-cycle counts)
answers.caveat: The 20-40 is a derived average for busy sites in Kaohsiung and New Taipei, not a counted queue at one red light; a particular junction can be well above or below it.

answers.question: What in scooter exhaust makes the smell, and at what concentrations do people smell it?
answers.bestAnswer: The smell is a mixture of unburnt petrol vapours (toluene and its relatives) and the sharp-smelling aldehydes made when fuel burns incompletely; weighing Taiwanese scooter exhaust against smell thresholds points to acetaldehyde, a fruity-pungent aldehyde noticed at about 1.5 parts per billion, as the strongest contributor, while carbon monoxide and ultrafine particles have no smell at all.
answers.bestAnswerZh: 氣味是一個混合物：一部分是沒燒完的汽油蒸氣（甲苯等），一部分是燃燒不完全產生的刺鼻醛類。把台灣機車廢氣的成分和「聞得到的門檻」放在一起比較，最可能最強烈的是乙醛（約十億分之 1.5 就聞得到，帶水果般的刺激味）；而一氧化碳和超細懸浮微粒完全沒有味道。

range.threshold_spread: other sources differ by 10-100x: acetaldehyde 0.05 ppm (EPA), formaldehyde 0.83 ppm (EPA) and 0.04-0.4 ppm (WHO 0.05-0.5 mg/m3), benzene 1.5 ppm (ATSDR) to 61-97 ppm (AIHA), acrolein 0.017 ppm (2017 olfactometer study, search summary only)

arithmetic: Threshold in mg/m3 = ppm x molecular weight / 24.45 (25 C): acetaldehyde 0.0015 x 44.05/24.45 = 0.0027; formaldehyde 0.50 x 30.03/24.45 = 0.614; toluene 0.33 x 92.14/24.45 = 1.24; isopentane 1.3 x 72.15/24.45 = 3.84; 2-methylpentane 7.0 x 86.18/24.45 = 24.7 mg/m3.

Odour load = emitted mg/km divided by threshold mg/m3 (clean air needed per km to dilute to the threshold). Emission inputs from Taiwanese Phase III motorcycle dynamometer tests (Tsai et al. 2003): toluene 30 (2-stroke) / 100 (4-stroke) mg/km; isopentane 53 / 295; 2-methylpentane 75 / 83; formaldehyde 0.4-0.7 mg/km; acetaldehyde 0.6-1.2 mg/km (the abstract summary I had does not say which engine type each carbonyl value belongs to, so the carbonyl inputs are given as the range). Results as above: acetaldehyde exceeds toluene by about 3 to 10 times and the dominant alkanes by 10 to 100 times; formaldehyde is negligible by this measure.

Not included because Taiwanese emission data were not available: acrolein (threshold 0.0036 ppm, 2.3x higher than acetaldehyde's) and the C9 alkylbenzenes with very low thresholds (n-propylbenzene 0.0038 ppm, p-ethyltoluene 0.0083 ppm, p-diethylbenzene 0.00039 ppm), which are part of petrol exhaust but unquantified in the sources I read.
answers.basis: Preference 3 (transparent estimate from measured quantities), not a sniff test. Inputs: Taiwanese dynamometer emission factors (Tsai 2003, abstract-level numbers verified by an earlier verifier) and Japanese triangle-odour-bag detection thresholds (Nagata, document opened and the table rows read). Outside support: Roy et al. (diesel direct-injection engines, SAE 2000-01-2820 and 2002-01-2875, search summaries) found exhaust odour correlated very well with aldehydes, formaldehyde most of all, and rose with low-boiling hydrocarbons; Vogh's older panel work found low aldehydes contributed little to diesel odour and a 1957 panel study found chemistry only weakly predicts odour, so the aldehyde story is plausible but not settled. A 1943 SAE bus study linked pungent gasoline-engine odour to aldehydes (search summary). No gas-chromatography-olfactometry study of scooter exhaust was found in English or Chinese searches. Two-stroke scooters add their own lubricant smoke smell (Platt 2014 shows two-strokes emit up to thousands of times the organic aerosol of other vehicles).
sources: Nagata Y. Measurement of odor threshold by triangle odor bag method, Japan Environmental Sanitation Center (223 substances, experiments 1976-1988), https://www.env.go.jp/content/900450144.pdf (opened: yes; thresholds above found in the tables)

Tsai J-H, Liu Y-Y, Yang C-Y, Chiang H-L, Chang L-P (2003) J. Air Waste Manag. Assoc. 53(5):516-522, doi:10.1080/10473289.2003.10466199, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12774984/ (numbers from research/redlight/smell-chemistry.json, verified there against the abstract; I could not reopen PubMed - it returned a cookie stub)
US EPA Hazard Summaries (benzene, formaldehyde, acetaldehyde), https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2016-09/documents/benzene.pdf (from earlier verifier)

WHO (2010) Guidelines for indoor air quality: selected pollutants, https://www.afro.who.int/sites/default/files/2017-06/e94535.pdf (from earlier verifier: CO odourless; formaldehyde odour 0.05-0.5 mg/m3)
Roy M M et al., SAE 2000-01-2820 https://saemobilus.sae.org/content/2000-01-2820/ and SAE 2002-01-2875 https://saemobilus.sae.org/content/2002-01-2875 (search summaries only; paywalled; opened: no)
Platt S M et al. (2014) Nature Communications 5:3749, https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms4749 (from earlier verifier)
answers.caveat: This ranks likely smell contributors from thresholds and emission rates; no one has smelled-and-analysed Taiwanese scooter exhaust, and real smell depends on the mixture, so treat acetaldehyde as the best candidate, not a proven main culprit.

findings.quote: The average idling emissions of pollutants CO, CO2, HC and NOx were 60.9, 534.3, 10.3 and 1.8 g/h, respectively. The average fuel loss during idling is around 180 g/h.
